### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.</description>

    25	If dbt is your source of truth for database schemas and you use Metabase as

    27	column descriptions and semantic types (e.g. currency, category, URL) to your

    30	Requirements
    31	============
    32	
    33	Requires Python 3.6 or above.
    34	
    35	Main features
    36	=============
    37	
    38	The main features provided by dbt-metabase are:
    39	
    40	* Parsing your dbt project (either through the ``manifest.json`` or directly through the YAML files)
    41	* Triggering a Metabase schema sync before propagating the metadata
    42	* Propagating table descriptions to Metabase
    43	* Propagating columns description to Metabase
    44	* Propagating columns semantic types and visibility types to Metabase through the use of dbt meta fields
    45	* Propagating table relationships represented as dbt ``relationships`` column tests
    46	* Extracting dbt model exposures from Metabase and generating YAML files to be included and revisioned with your dbt deployment
    47	
    48	
    49	Usage
    50	=====
    51	
    52	You can install dbt-metabase from `PyPI`_:
    53	
    54	.. _`PyPI`: https://pypi.org/project/dbt-metabase/
    55	
    56	.. code-block:: shell
    57	
    58	    pip install dbt-metabase
    59	
    60	Sections below demonstrate basic usage examples, for all CLI options:
    61	
    62	.. code-block:: shell
    63	
    64	    dbt-metabase --help
    65	
    66	When invoking programmatically, click through to implementation and refer to header comments.
    67	
    68	Basic Example
    69	-------------
    70	
    71	Let's start by defining a short sample ``schema.yml`` as below.
    72	
    73	.. code-block:: yaml
    74	
    75	    models:
    76	      - name: stg_users
    77	        description: User records.
    78	        columns:
    79	          - name: id
    80	            description: Primary key.
    81	            tests:
    82	              - not_null
    83	              - unique
    84	          - name: email
    85	            description: User's email address.
    86	          - name: group_id
    87	            description: Foreign key to user group.
    88	            tests:
    89	              - not_null
    90	              - relationships:
    91	                  to: ref('groups')
    92	                  field: id
    93	
    94	      - name: stg_groups
    95	        description: User groups.
    96	        columns:
    97	          - name: id
    98	            description: Primary key.
    99	            tests:
   100	              - not_null
   101	              - unique
   102	          - name: name
   103	            description: Group name.
   104	
   105	That's already enough to propagate the primary keys, foreign keys and
   106	descriptions to Metabase by executing the below command.
   107	
   108	.. code-block:: shell
   109	
   110	    dbt-metabase models \
   111	        --dbt_path . \
   112	        --dbt_database business \
   113	        --metabase_host metabase.example.com \
   114	        --metabase_user user@example.com \
   115	        --metabase_password Password123 \
   116	        --metabase_database business \
   117	        --dbt_schema public
   118	
   119	Check your Metabase instance by going into Settings > Admin > Data Model, you
   120	will notice that ``ID`` in ``STG_USERS`` is now marked as "Entity Key" and
   121	``GROUP_ID`` is marked as "Foreign Key" pointing to ``ID`` in ``STG_GROUPS``.

   124	-------------------
   125	
   126	dbt-metabase also allows us to extract exposures from Metabase. The invocation is almost identical to
   127	our models function with the addition of output name and location args. `dbt exposures`_ let us understand
   128	how our dbt models are exposed in BI which closes the loop between ELT, modelling, and consumption.
   129	
   130	
   131	.. _`dbt exposures`: https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/building-a-dbt-project/exposures
   132	
   133	
   134	.. code-block:: shell
   135	
   136	    dbt-metabase exposures \
   137	        --dbt_manifest_path ./target/manifest.json \
   138	        --dbt_database business \
   139	        --metabase_host metabase.example.com \
   140	        --metabase_user user@example.com \
   141	        --metabase_password Password123 \
   142	        --metabase_database business \
   143	        --output_path ./models/ \
   144	        --output_name metabase_exposures
   145	
   146	Once execution completes, a look at the output ``metabase_exposures.yml`` will
   147	reveal all metabase exposures documented with the documentation, descriptions, creator
   148	emails & names, links to exposures, and even native SQL propagated over from Metabase.

   157	          A line chart depicting how order volume changes over time
   158

   177	on a cadence every X days) in order to keep a dbt docs site fully synchronized with BI. This makes ``dbt docs`` a
   178	useful utility for introspecting the data model from source -> consumption with zero extra/repeated human input.

   180	Reading your dbt project
   181	------------------------
   182	
   183	There are two approaches provided by this library to read your dbt project:
   184	
   185	1. Artifacts
   186	^^^^^^^^^^^^
   187	
   188	You can instruct dbt-metabase to read your ``manifest.json``, a `dbt artifact`_ containing 
   189	the full representation of your dbt project's resources. If your dbt project uses multiple schemas, 
   190	multiple databases or model aliases, you must use this approach.
   191	
   192	Note that you you have to run ``dbt compile --target prod`` or any of the other dbt commands
   193	listed in the dbt documentation above to get a fresh copy of your ``manifest.json``. Remember
   194	to run it against your production target.
   195	
   196	When using the ``dbt-metabase`` CLI, you must provide a ``--dbt_manifest_path`` argument
   197	pointing to your ``manifest.json`` file (usually in the ``target/`` folder of your dbt
   198	project).
   199	
   200	.. _`dbt artifact`: https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/artifacts/dbt-artifacts
   201	
   202	2. Direct parsing
   203	^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   204	
   205	Alternatively, you can provide the path to your dbt project root folder using the argument
   206	``--dbt_path``. dbt-metabase will then look for all .yml files and parse your documentation
   207	and tests directly from there. It does not support dbt projects with custom schemas.

   209	Semantic Types
   210	--------------
   211	
   212	Now that we have primary and foreign keys, let's tell Metabase that ``email``
   213	column contains email addresses.
   214	
   215	Change the ``email`` column as follows:
   216	
   217	.. code-block:: yaml
   218	
   219	    - name: email
   220	      description: User's email address.
   221	      meta:
   222	        metabase.semantic_type: type/Email
   223	
   224	Once you run ``dbt-metabase models`` again, you will notice that ``EMAIL`` is
   225	now marked as "Email".
   226	
   227	Here are common semantic types (formerly known as special types) accepted by Metabase:
   228	
   229	* ``type/PK``
   230	* ``type/FK``
   231	* ``type/Number``
   232	* ``type/Currency``
   233	* ``type/Category``
   234	* ``type/Title``
   235	* ``type/Description``
   236	* ``type/City``
   237	* ``type/State``
   238	* ``type/ZipCode``
   239	* ``type/Country``
   240	* ``type/Latitude``
   241	* ``type/Longitude``
   242	* ``type/Email``
   243	* ``type/URL``
   244	* ``type/ImageURL``
   245	* ``type/SerializedJSON``
   246	* ``type/CreationTimestamp``
   247	
   248	See `documentation`_ for a more complete list.
   249	
   250	.. _`documentation`: https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/users-guide/field-types.html
   251	
   252	Foreign Keys
   253	------------
   254	
   255	Built-in relationship tests are the recommended way of defining foreign keys,
   256	however you can alternatively use ``fk_target_table`` and ``fk_target_field``
   257	meta fields (``semantic_type`` is optional and will be inferred). If both are 
   258	set for a column, meta fields take precedence.
   259	
   260	.. code-block:: yaml
   261	
   262	    - name: country_id
   263	      description: FK to User's country in the dim_countries table.
   264	      meta:
   265	        metabase.semantic_type: type/FK
   266	        metabase.fk_target_table: analytics_dims.dim_countries
   267	        metabase.fk_target_field: id
   268	
   269	You can provide ``fk_target_table`` in the format ``schema_name.table_name`` or
   270	just ``table_name`` to use the current schema. If your model has an alias, provide
   271	that alias (rather than the original name).
   272	
   273	Visibility Types
   274	----------------
   275	
   276	In addition to semantic types, you can optionally specify visibility for each
   277	table and field. This affects whether or not they are displayed in the Metabase UI.
   278	
   279	Here is how you would hide that same email:
   280	
   281	.. code-block:: yaml
   282	
   283	    - name: email
   284	      description: User's email address.
   285	      meta:
   286	        metabase.semantic_type: type/Email
   287	        metabase.visibility_type: sensitive
   288	
   289	Here are the field visibility types supported by Metabase:
   290	
   291	* ``normal`` (default)
   292	* ``details-only``
   293	* ``sensitive``
   294	
   295	Tables only support the following:
   296	
   297	* No value for visible (default)
   298	* ``hidden``
   299	* ``technical``
   300	* ``cruft``
   301	
   302	If you notice new ones, please submit a PR to update this readme.
   303	
   304	Model Extra Fields
   305	------------------
   306	
   307	In addition to the model description, Metabase accepts two extra information fields. Those optional
   308	fields are called ``caveats`` and ``points_of_interest`` and can be defined under the ``meta`` tag
   309	of the model.
   310	
   311	This is how you can specify them in the ``stg_users`` example:
   312	
   313	.. code-block:: yaml
   314	
   315	  - name: stg_users
   316	    description: User records.
   317	    meta:
   318	      metabase.points_of_interest: Relevant records.
   319	      metabase.caveats: Sensitive information about users.
   320

   322	Database Sync
   323	-------------
   324	
   325	By default, dbt-metabase will tell Metabase to synchronize database fields
   326	and wait for the data model to contain all the tables and columns in your dbt
   327	project.
   328	
   329	You can control this behavior with two arguments:
   330	
   331	* ``--metabase_sync_skip`` - boolean to optionally disable pre-synchronization
   332	* ``--metabase_sync_timeout`` - number of seconds to wait and re-check data model before
   333	  giving up
   334	
   335	Configuration
   336	-------------
   337

class StripCommentsFilter(object):
    @staticmethod
    def _process(tlist):
        def get_next_comment():
            # TODO(andi) Comment types should be unified, see related issue38
            return tlist.token_next_by(i=sql.Comment, t=T.Comment)

        tidx, token = get_next_comment()
        while token:
            pidx, prev_ = tlist.token_prev(tidx, skip_ws=False)
            nidx, next_ = tlist.token_next(tidx, skip_ws=False)
            # Replace by whitespace if prev and next exist and if they're not
            # whitespaces. This doesn't apply if prev or next is a parenthesis.
            if (prev_ is None or next_ is None or
                    prev_.is_whitespace or prev_.match(T.Punctuation, '(') or
                    next_.is_whitespace or next_.match(T.Punctuation, ')')):
                tlist.tokens.remove(token)
            else:
                tlist.tokens[tidx] = sql.Token(T.Whitespace, ' ')

            tidx, token = get_next_comment()

    def process(self, stmt):
        [self.process(sgroup) for sgroup in stmt.get_sublists()]
        StripCommentsFilter._process(stmt)
        return stmt
